questions.question: The relation $R$ on set $A$ is called empty relation if and only if
questions.answer:
**(A)** $R=\phi$

**Step 1 — what a relation on $A$ is.** A relation $R$ on a set $A$ is any *subset* of $A\times A$, so the possible relations run from the smallest subset to the largest:
$$\phi\ \subseteq\ R\ \subseteq\ A\times A$$

**Step 2 — the smallest subset.** A relation is called **empty (void) relation** exactly when no element of $A$ is related to any element, i.e. when
$$R=\phi$$

$$\therefore\ R=\phi\ \text{— option (A)}$$

**Why the others fail:**

- $R=A$ is not even a subset of $A\times A$ in general (it can only be a relation if $A\subseteq A\times A$, which never happens for a non-empty set) ✗
- $R=A\times A$ is the **universal relation**: every element is related to every element, the opposite extreme ✗

**Illustration:** for $A=\{1,2\}$, the empty relation is $\phi$ (nothing related), while $A\times A=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(2,2)\}$ is the universal relation. The empty relation is vacuously symmetric and transitive, but not reflexive on a non-empty set.

questions.question: If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x)=6x-5$ then $f^{-1}(x)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{x+5}{6}$

**Step 1 — write $y=f(x)$:**
$$y=6x-5$$

**Step 2 — solve for $x$:**
$$6x=y+5\ \Rightarrow\ x=\frac{y+5}{6}$$

**Step 3 — interchange $x$ and $y$:**
$$f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x+5}{6}$$

**Check both ways:**
$$f\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=6\cdot\frac{x+5}{6}-5=x+5-5=x\ ✓$$
$$f^{-1}\left(f(x)\right)=\frac{(6x-5)+5}{6}=\frac{6x}{6}=x\ ✓$$

**Why (B) fails:** $\dfrac{x-5}{6}$ would be correct for $f(x)=6x+5$; the sign of the constant flips when we transpose it. Testing $x=1$: $f(1)=1$, and the correct inverse must return $1$; $\dfrac{1-5}{6}=-\dfrac23\neq1$ ✗, while $\dfrac{1+5}{6}=1$ ✓.

questions.question: If $y=\cos^{-1}x$ then
questions.answer:
**(A)** $0\le y\le\pi$

**Step 1 — the definition of the principal branch.** The inverse cosine is defined by restricting $\cos$ to $[0,\pi]$, the largest interval on which it is one-one. Hence
$$y=\cos^{-1}x\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \cos y=x\ \text{and}\ y\in[0,\pi]$$

$$\therefore\ 0\le y\le\pi\ \text{— option (A)}$$

**Why the others fail:**

- $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le y\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is the range of $\sin^{-1}$ and $\tan^{-1}$, not of $\cos^{-1}$ ✗
- $-\pi\le y\le\pi$ is a full period of cosine; on that interval $\cos$ takes most values twice (e.g. $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac12$), so it is not one-one and cannot define an inverse ✗

**Endpoint check:** $\cos^{-1}(1)=0$, $\cos^{-1}(0)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\cos^{-1}(-1)=\pi$ ✓ — the whole interval $[0,\pi]$ is covered exactly once.

**Note on the printed key:** the tick in the booklet sits beside (C) $-\pi\le y\le\pi$, which cannot be right for a one-one branch. The correct range is (A).

**Compare the three principal ranges:**
$$\sin^{-1}x:\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right],\qquad \cos^{-1}x:[0,\pi],\qquad \tan^{-1}x:\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$

questions.question: Principal value of $\tan^{-1}(-1)$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

**Step 1 — the principal range** of $\tan^{-1}$ is $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

**Step 2 — use oddness,** $\tan^{-1}(-t)=-\tan^{-1}t$:
$$\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\tan^{-1}(1)$$

**Step 3 — the angle in the principal range** with tangent $1$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\therefore\ \tan^{-1}(-1)=-\frac{\pi}{4}$$

**Check:** $\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=-1$ ✓ and $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ ✓.

**Why (C) fails:** $\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=-1$ is true, but $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=135^{\circ}$ lies outside the principal range, so it is not the *principal* value.

**Why (A) fails:** $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}=+1\neq-1$ — the sign is ignored.

questions.question: If $\begin{bmatrix}x+y\\ y+z\\ z+x\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\\ -1\end{bmatrix}$ then $x+y+z=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $0$

**Step 1 — equal column matrices have equal entries:**
$$x+y=1\qquad\ldots(1)$$
$$y+z=0\qquad\ldots(2)$$
$$z+x=-1\qquad\ldots(3)$$

**Step 2 — add all three equations.** Each of $x,y,z$ appears exactly twice:
$$(x+y)+(y+z)+(z+x)=1+0+(-1)$$
$$2x+2y+2z=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2(x+y+z)=0$$

**Step 3 — divide by $2$:**
$$x+y+z=0$$

$$\therefore\ x+y+z=0\ \text{— option (B)}$$

**The individual values (for a check):** from (1) $z=(x+y+z)-(x+y)=0-1=-1$; from (2) $x=0-0=0$; from (3) $y=0-(-1)=1$. So $(x,y,z)=(0,1,-1)$, and indeed $0+1-1=0$ ✓, $x+y=1$ ✓, $y+z=0$ ✓, $z+x=-1$ ✓.

**Why the big numbers in the options are irrelevant:** the sum telescopes — no matter what the right-hand column is, adding the three rows always gives $2(x+y+z)$.

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\ 1&3\end{bmatrix}$ then $A^{2}=$
questions.answer:
**(D)** None of these

**Step 1 — multiply $A$ by itself,** row times column:
$$A^{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\ 1&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\ 1&3\end{bmatrix}$$

**Entry $(1,1)$:** $(2)(2)+(4)(1)=4+4=8$

**Entry $(1,2)$:** $(2)(4)+(4)(3)=8+12=20$

**Entry $(2,1)$:** $(1)(2)+(3)(1)=2+3=5$

**Entry $(2,2)$:** $(1)(4)+(3)(3)=4+9=13$

$$\therefore\ A^{2}=\begin{bmatrix}8&20\\ 5&13\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — compare with the options.** None of $\begin{bmatrix}4&16\\ 9&1\end{bmatrix}$, $\begin{bmatrix}2&12\\ 6&2\end{bmatrix}$, $\begin{bmatrix}16&13\\ 9&12\end{bmatrix}$ equals $\begin{bmatrix}8&20\\ 5&13\end{bmatrix}$, so the answer is **(D)** None of these.

**Why (A) is the tempting trap:** it is obtained by **squaring each entry separately** ($2^{2}=4$, $4^{2}=16$, $1^{2}=1$, $3^{2}=9$) — but matrix multiplication is not entrywise.

**Consistency check:** $\det A=6-4=2$, so $\det\left(A^{2}\right)=2^{2}=4$; and $\det\begin{bmatrix}8&20\\ 5&13\end{bmatrix}=104-100=4$ ✓.

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&x+2\\ 2x-3&x+1\end{bmatrix}$ is symmetric matrix then $x=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $5$

**Step 1 — the definition of symmetry:** $A^{\mathsf T}=A$, i.e. $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$ for every pair. For a $2\times2$ matrix this is the single condition
$$a_{12}=a_{21}$$

**Step 2 — substitute the entries:**
$$x+2=2x-3$$

**Step 3 — solve:**
$$x+2=2x-3\ \Rightarrow\ 5=x$$

$$\therefore\ x=5$$

**Check:** with $x=5$,
$$A=\begin{bmatrix}4&7\\ 7&6\end{bmatrix},\qquad A^{\mathsf T}=\begin{bmatrix}4&7\\ 7&6\end{bmatrix}=A\ ✓$$
The diagonal entries $4$ and $6$ are unrestricted — symmetry never constrains them.

**Why the other options fail:** at $x=3$, $a_{12}=5$ but $a_{21}=3$ ✗; at $x=4$, $a_{12}=6$ but $a_{21}=5$ ✗.

questions.question: If $\begin{vmatrix}x&3\\ 8&x\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}6&2\\ 18&2\end{vmatrix}$ then $x=$
questions.answer:
**(D)** None of these

**Step 1 — expand the left determinant:**
$$\begin{vmatrix}x&3\\ 8&x\end{vmatrix}=x\cdot x-3\cdot8=x^{2}-24$$

**Step 2 — expand the right determinant:**
$$\begin{vmatrix}6&2\\ 18&2\end{vmatrix}=6\cdot2-2\cdot18=12-36=-24$$

**Step 3 — equate the two:**
$$x^{2}-24=-24\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=0$$

**Step 4 — compare with the options.** $x=0$ is not $\sqrt{24}$, $-\sqrt{24}$ or $\pm\sqrt{24}$, so the answer is **(D)** None of these.

**Check:** with $x=0$ the left determinant is $\begin{vmatrix}0&3\\ 8&0\end{vmatrix}=-24$, equal to the right side $-24$ ✓.

**Why $\pm\sqrt{24}$ is the tempting trap:** that value solves the *different* equation $\begin{vmatrix}x&3\\ 8&x\end{vmatrix}=0$, i.e. $x^{2}=24$. It would be the answer if the right-hand determinant were $0$ (for instance $\begin{vmatrix}6&2\\ 18&6\end{vmatrix}$). Here the right side is $-24$, which cancels the $-24$ in $x^{2}-24$ and leaves $x=0$.

questions.question: $\begin{vmatrix}\cos30^{\circ}&\sin30^{\circ}\\ \sin30^{\circ}&\cos30^{\circ}\end{vmatrix}=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac12$

**Step 1 — expand the determinant:**
$$\begin{vmatrix}\cos30^{\circ}&\sin30^{\circ}\\ \sin30^{\circ}&\cos30^{\circ}\end{vmatrix}=\cos^{2}30^{\circ}-\sin^{2}30^{\circ}$$

**Step 2 — recognise the double-angle identity:** $\cos^{2}\theta-\sin^{2}\theta=\cos2\theta$, so with $\theta=30^{\circ}$:
$$=\cos60^{\circ}=\frac12$$

**Step 3 — verify numerically.** $\cos30^{\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\sin30^{\circ}=\dfrac12$:
$$\frac34-\frac14=\frac12\ ✓$$

$$\therefore\ \text{determinant}=\frac12$$

**Structure note:** the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $\cos2\theta$; for $\theta=30^{\circ}$ this is $\cos60^{\circ}=\dfrac12$.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\cos3x\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $-3\sin3x$

**Step 1 — chain rule** with $u=3x$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\cos u=-\sin u\cdot\frac{du}{dx}$$

**Step 2 — differentiate the inside:** $\dfrac{du}{dx}=3$, so
$$\frac{d}{dx}\cos3x=-\sin3x\cdot3=-3\sin3x$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}\cos3x=-3\sin3x$$

**Why each distractor is wrong:** (A) omits the inner derivative $3$; (C) forgets to differentiate at all; (D) keeps $\cos$ where the derivative of $\cos$ is $-\sin$.

**Check at $x=0$:** $\cos3x$ has a maximum there, so its slope must be $0$; the formula gives $-3\sin0=0$ ✓. Near $x=0$, $\cos3x\approx1-\dfrac{9x^{2}}{2}$, whose derivative $-9x$ matches $-3\sin3x\approx-9x$ ✓.

**General rule worth memorising:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\cos(ax)=-a\sin(ax),\qquad \frac{d}{dx}\sin(ax)=a\cos(ax)$$

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\left(x^{2}\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{2x}{1+x^{4}}$

**Step 1 — chain rule** with $u=x^{2}$, using $\dfrac{d}{du}\tan^{-1}u=\dfrac{1}{1+u^{2}}$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\left(x^{2}\right)=\frac{1}{1+\left(x^{2}\right)^{2}}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2}\right)$$

**Step 2 — simplify.** The square of the argument is $\left(x^{2}\right)^{2}=x^{4}$, and the inner derivative is $2x$:
$$=\frac{1}{1+x^{4}}\cdot2x=\frac{2x}{1+x^{4}}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\left(x^{2}\right)=\frac{2x}{1+x^{4}}$$

**Why (B) fails:** $\dfrac{x}{1+x^{2}}$ drops a factor $2$ and squares the wrong quantity — it would be the derivative of $\dfrac12\tan^{-1}$-type combinations of $x^{2}$ handled sloppily, and the denominator must be $1+\left(\text{argument}\right)^{2}=1+x^{4}$.

**Check at $x=1$:** the formula gives $\dfrac{2}{1+1}=1$. Numerical sense: $\tan^{-1}\left(x^{2}\right)$ rises steeply near $0$ (slope $2x\to0$ at the origin but growing) and its slope at $1$ equals exactly $1$ ✓.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{\sin x}\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $e^{\sin x}\cdot\cos x$

**Step 1 — chain rule** with $u=\sin x$, using $\dfrac{d}{du}e^{u}=e^{u}$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{\sin x}=e^{\sin x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sin x\right)$$

**Step 2 — differentiate the inside:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$, so
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{\sin x}=e^{\sin x}\cos x$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}e^{\sin x}=e^{\sin x}\cos x$$

**Why the others fail:** (B) forgets the inner derivative entirely; (C) drops the exponential factor; both would fail the product-rule structure that composition demands.

**Check at $x=0$:** $e^{\sin x}\approx e^{x}\approx1+x$, so the slope at $0$ is $1$; the formula gives $e^{0}\cos0=1$ ✓.

**General rule:** for any differentiable $u$,
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{u}=e^{u}\frac{du}{dx}$$
which is the reason $e^{x}$ is its own derivative only when $u=x$.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log\sec x\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\tan x$

**Step 1 — chain rule** with $u=\sec x$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\log\left(\sec x\right)=\frac{1}{\sec x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sec x\right)$$

**Step 2 — the derivative of secant** is $\sec x\tan x$, so
$$=\frac{1}{\sec x}\cdot\sec x\tan x=\tan x$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}\left(\log\sec x\right)=\tan x$$

**Why (B) fails:** $\cot x$ would arise from $\log\sin x$, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log\sin x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\cot x$.

**Useful consequence:** since $\log\sec x=-\log\cos x$, the same result reads $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\log\cos x\right)=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\tan x$ ✓ — a neat cross-check.

**And the standard integral that follows:**
$$\int\tan x\,dx=\log\left|\sec x\right|+C$$
which is why the formula is worth remembering.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{\tan^{-1}x}\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^{2}}$

**Step 1 — chain rule** with $u=\tan^{-1}x$, using $\dfrac{d}{du}e^{u}=e^{u}$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{\tan^{-1}x}=e^{\tan^{-1}x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan^{-1}x\right)$$

**Step 2 — the inner derivative:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}x=\dfrac{1}{1+x^{2}}$, so
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{\tan^{-1}x}=\frac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^{2}}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{\tan^{-1}x}\right)=\frac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^{2}}$$

**Why (C) fails:** it forgets the exponential factor $e^{\tan^{-1}x}$ — the outer function must be retained in the chain rule.

**Check at $x=0$:** $e^{\tan^{-1}x}\approx e^{x}\approx1+x$, so the slope at $0$ should be $1$; the formula gives $\dfrac{e^{0}}{1+0}=1$ ✓.

**General pattern:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{f(x)}=e^{f(x)}f'(x)$$
so the answer always keeps the exponential and multiplies by the derivative of the exponent.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(a^{x}\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $a^{x}\log a$

**Step 1 — write the exponential with base $e$.** Since $a=e^{\log a}$,
$$a^{x}=e^{x\log a}$$

**Step 2 — differentiate by the chain rule** (the exponent is $x\log a$, a constant multiple of $x$):
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{x\log a}=e^{x\log a}\cdot\log a=a^{x}\log a$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}a^{x}=a^{x}\log a$$

**Why the others fail:** (B) $\log a$ forgets the factor $a^{x}$; (C) $a^{x}$ is correct only in the special case $a=e$, where $\log e=1$.

**Check with $a=2$:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}2^{x}=2^{x}\log2\approx0\cdot693\cdot2^{x}$; numerically, $2^{x}$ grows at about $69\%$ of its own value per unit $x$ (the doubling time is $\dfrac{\log2}{\log2}=1$ unit, and $\log2\approx0\cdot693$) ✓.

**Contrast with the power rule:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}x^{a}=ax^{a-1}$ (variable base, constant exponent) while $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^{x}=a^{x}\log a$ (constant base, variable exponent) — the two are often confused.

questions.question: If $x=a\cos\theta$, $y=a\sin\theta$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.answer:
**(A)** $-\cot\theta$

**Step 1 — differentiate each equation with respect to $\theta$:**
$$\frac{dx}{d\theta}=-a\sin\theta,\qquad \frac{dy}{d\theta}=a\cos\theta$$

**Step 2 — apply** $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{a\cos\theta}{-a\sin\theta}=-\cot\theta$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\cot\theta$$

**Why (C) fails:** the factor $a$ cancels — the parameter $a$ is the radius and disappears from the slope.

**Geometric check.** The equations describe the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=a^{2}$. Differentiating implicitly,
$$2x+2y\frac{dy}{dx}=0\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac xy=-\frac{a\cos\theta}{a\sin\theta}=-\cot\theta\ ✓$$

**Sanity check at $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:** the point is $\left(\dfrac{a}{\sqrt2},\dfrac{a}{\sqrt2}\right)$ and the radius there makes $45^{\circ}$ with the $x$-axis; the tangent is perpendicular to the radius, so its slope must be $-1$. The formula gives $-\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=-1$ ✓.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\sin(2x+3)\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $-\dfrac{\cos(2x+3)}{2}+C$

**Step 1 — substitute** $u=2x+3$, so $du=2\,dx$, i.e. $dx=\dfrac{du}{2}$:
$$\int\sin(2x+3)dx=\frac12\int\sin u\,du$$

**Step 2 — integrate** using $\displaystyle\int\sin u\,du=-\cos u$:
$$=\frac12\left(-\cos u\right)+C=-\frac{\cos(2x+3)}{2}+C$$

$$\therefore\ \int\sin(2x+3)dx=-\frac{\cos(2x+3)}{2}+C$$

**Check by differentiating:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[-\frac{\cos(2x+3)}{2}\right]=-\frac12\left(-\sin(2x+3)\right)\cdot2=\sin(2x+3)\ ✓$$

**Why (A) fails:** $\cos(2x+3)$ differentiates to $-2\sin(2x+3)$, which is off by a factor $-2$ — the sign and the constant $2$ both matter.

**General rule:**
$$\int\sin(ax+b)dx=-\frac{\cos(ax+b)}{a}+C,\qquad \int\cos(ax+b)dx=\frac{\sin(ax+b)}{a}+C$$

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\tan^{2}x\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\tan x-x+C$

**Step 1 — use the identity** $\tan^{2}x=\sec^{2}x-1$:
$$\int\tan^{2}x\,dx=\int\left(\sec^{2}x-1\right)dx$$

**Step 2 — integrate term by term,** recalling $\displaystyle\int\sec^{2}x\,dx=\tan x$:
$$=\tan x-x+C$$

$$\therefore\ \int\tan^{2}x\,dx=\tan x-x+C$$

**Check by differentiating:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan x-x\right)=\sec^{2}x-1=\tan^{2}x\ ✓$$

**Why (B) fails:** $\tan x+x$ differentiates to $\sec^{2}x+1$, which is $\tan^{2}x+2$ — off by $2$.

**Why (A) fails:** the derivative of $\cot x-x$ is $-\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x-1$, the negative of $\cot^{2}x+2$-type expression; it has nothing to do with $\tan^{2}x$.

**Sanity check with signs:** $\tan^{2}x\ge0$ everywhere, so the antiderivative must be increasing; $\tan x-x$ has derivative $\tan^{2}x\ge0$ ✓, and it vanishes to second order at $x=0$ where $\tan^{2}x\approx x^{2}$ — consistent with $\tan x-x\approx\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}$ ✓.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^{2}+16}=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac14\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac x4\right)+C$

**Step 1 — the standard form** $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac xa+C$.

**Step 2 — identify $a$.** Here $16=a^{2}$, so $a=4$:
$$\int\frac{dx}{x^{2}+16}=\frac14\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x4\right)+C$$

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{dx}{x^{2}+16}=\frac14\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x4\right)+C$$

**Check by differentiating:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac14\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x4\right)\right]=\frac14\cdot\frac{1}{1+\frac{x^{2}}{16}}\cdot\frac14=\frac{1}{16}\cdot\frac{16}{16+x^{2}}=\frac{1}{x^{2}+16}\ ✓$$

**Why (C) fails:** it uses $a=2$, i.e. $x^{2}+4$ in the denominator, not $x^{2}+16$.

**Why (B) fails:** it forgets the factor $\dfrac1a$ entirely.

**Mnemonic:** the constant out front is the *reciprocal of the square root* of the constant term: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16}}=\dfrac14$ ✓.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1+\cos2x}\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(D)** None of these

**Step 1 — simplify the integrand** with $1+\cos2x=2\cos^{2}x$:
$$\sqrt{1+\cos2x}=\sqrt{2\cos^{2}x}=\sqrt2\left|\cos x\right|$$

On $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ we have $\cos x\ge0$, so $\left|\cos x\right|=\cos x$ and the integrand is $\sqrt2\cos x$.

**Step 2 — integrate:**
$$I=\sqrt2\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx=\sqrt2\left[\sin x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}=\sqrt2(1-0)=\sqrt2$$

$$\therefore\ I=\sqrt2\approx1\cdot414$$

**Step 3 — compare with the options.** $\sqrt2$ is not $0$, not $1$, not $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so the answer is **(D)** None of these.

**Check numerically:** averaging $\sqrt{1+\cos2x}$ over $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ — at $x=0$ it is $\sqrt2\approx1\cdot414$, at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ it is $\sqrt{1+0}=1$, at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ it is $0$ — an average around $0\cdot9$, times the length $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\approx1\cdot571$ gives about $1\cdot41$ ✓.

**Note on the printed key:** the tick in the booklet sits beside (D) — that is correct, since $\sqrt2$ is genuinely absent from the list. Beware (C) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, which is the reciprocal of the right answer.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e}\frac{\left(\log x\right)^{2}}{x}\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\dfrac13$

**Step 1 — substitute** $t=\log x$, so $dt=\dfrac{dx}{x}$. The integrand is exactly $t^{2}\,dt$.

**Step 2 — change the limits:** $x=1\Rightarrow t=\log1=0$; $x=e\Rightarrow t=\log e=1$.

**Step 3 — integrate:**
$$I=\int_{0}^{1}t^{2}dt=\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}=\frac13-0=\frac13$$

$$\therefore\ I=\frac13$$

**Why (B) fails:** $\dfrac13\left(e^{3}-1\right)$ would come from integrating $t^{2}$ between $t=0$ and $t=3$ (or from forgetting to convert the limits) — the limits in $t$ are $0$ and $1$, not $0$ and $3$.

**Check by a different route.** An antiderivative is $\dfrac{\left(\log x\right)^{3}}{3}$, so
$$\left[\frac{\left(\log x\right)^{3}}{3}\right]_{1}^{e}=\frac{1^{3}}{3}-\frac{0^{3}}{3}=\frac13\ ✓$$

**Answer warning:** the answer $\dfrac13$ looks small, but the integrand $\dfrac{\left(\log x\right)^{2}}{x}$ is at most $\dfrac{1}{e}$ on $[1,e]$ (its peak at $x=e$ is $\dfrac{1}{e}\approx0\cdot37$), so an integral of $\dfrac13$ over a length of about $1\cdot7$ is entirely reasonable ✓.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int e^{x}\left(\log\sec x+\tan x\right)dx=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $e^{x}\left(\log\sec x\right)+C$

**Step 1 — use the standard form** $\displaystyle\int e^{x}\left[f(x)+f'(x)\right]dx=e^{x}f(x)+C$.

**Step 2 — identify $f$.** Take $f(x)=\log\sec x$; then
$$f'(x)=\tan x$$
which is precisely the second term in the bracket.

**Step 3 — apply the formula:**
$$\int e^{x}\left(\log\sec x+\tan x\right)dx=e^{x}\log\left(\sec x\right)+C$$

$$\therefore\ \int e^{x}\left(\log\sec x+\tan x\right)dx=e^{x}\left(\log\sec x\right)+C$$

**Check by differentiating (product rule):**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[e^{x}\log\sec x\right]=e^{x}\log\sec x+e^{x}\cdot\tan x=e^{x}\left(\log\sec x+\tan x\right)\ ✓$$

**Why (A) and (B) fail:** both differentiate to $e^{x}$ times something unrelated — e.g. $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x}\tan x\right)=e^{x}\left(\tan x+\sec^{2}x\right)\neq e^{x}\left(\log\sec x+\tan x\right)$.

**The general identity in action:**
$$\int e^{x}\left[f(x)+f'(x)\right]dx=e^{x}f(x)+C$$
is worth memorising — it converts a two-term integrand into a one-line answer whenever the second term is the derivative of the first.

questions.question: The order of the differential equation $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}}$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $2$

**Step 1 — recall the definitions.**
$$\text{Order}=\text{highest derivative present},\qquad \text{Degree}=\text{power of that highest derivative (after clearing radicals)}$$

**Step 2 — find the highest derivative.** The equation contains $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$; the highest is the second derivative.

$$\therefore\ \text{order}=2\ \text{— option (B)}$$

**Note on the degree (a common follow-up).** As printed the equation has a square root, so the degree is not defined until the radical is removed. Squaring both sides:
$$\left(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right)^{2}=1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}$$
Now the highest derivative appears with power $2$, so the **degree is $2$**.

**Contrast:** $\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}+y=0$ has order $3$, degree $1$; $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{4}+y=0$ has order $1$, degree $4$ — the order never changes when the equation is squared, only the degree does.

questions.question: If $\vec a=2\hat i-7\hat j-3\hat k$ then $\hat a=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{2\hat i-7\hat j-3\hat k}{\sqrt{62}}$

**Step 1 — the magnitude:**
$$\left|\vec a\right|=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-7)^{2}+(-3)^{2}}=\sqrt{4+49+9}=\sqrt{62}$$

**Step 2 — divide the vector by its magnitude:**
$$\hat a=\frac{\vec a}{\left|\vec a\right|}=\frac{2\hat i-7\hat j-3\hat k}{\sqrt{62}}$$

$$\therefore\ \hat a=\frac{2\hat i-7\hat j-3\hat k}{\sqrt{62}}$$

**Verify the result is a unit vector:**
$$\left|\hat a\right|=\frac{\sqrt{4+49+9}}{\sqrt{62}}=\frac{\sqrt{62}}{\sqrt{62}}=1\ ✓$$

**Why (B) fails:** $2\hat i-7\hat j-3\hat k$ has magnitude $\sqrt{62}\approx7\cdot87$, far from $1$ — it is the vector itself, not its direction.

**Why (C) fails:** $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{62}}$ is a *scalar*; a unit vector must retain the direction (the $\hat i,\hat j,\hat k$ components).

**Decimal form for intuition:** $\sqrt{62}\approx7\cdot874$, so
$$\hat a\approx0\cdot254\hat i-0\cdot889\hat j-0\cdot381\hat k$$
and indeed $0\cdot254^{2}+0\cdot889^{2}+0\cdot381^{2}\approx0\cdot065+0\cdot790+0\cdot145=1\cdot00$ ✓.

questions.question: For what value of $x$, vectors $x\hat i-3\hat j-5\hat k$ and $-\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$ are perpendicular to each other?
questions.answer:
**(C)** $-13$

**Step 1 — perpendicular means zero dot product:**
$$\left(x\hat i-3\hat j-5\hat k\right)\cdot\left(-\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k\right)=0$$

**Step 2 — compute the dot product:**
$$x(-1)+(-3)(1)+(-5)(2)=0$$
$$-x-3-10=0$$

**Step 3 — solve:**
$$-x-13=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=-13$$

$$\therefore\ x=-13$$

**Check:** with $x=-13$ the first vector is $-13\hat i-3\hat j-5\hat k$, and
$$\left(-13\hat i-3\hat j-5\hat k\right)\cdot\left(-\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k\right)=13-3-10=0\ ✓$$

**Careful with signs:** the two negative components of the first vector and the mixed signs of the second are the whole point of the question — a single sign slip gives $x=7$ or $x=4$.

**Geometric meaning:** $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a||\vec b|}=0$ means $\theta=90^{\circ}$, i.e. the vectors meet at a right angle.

questions.question: Find the projection of vector $\vec a=2\hat i+3\hat j+2\hat k$ on the vector $\vec b=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$.
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt6}$

**Step 1 — the projection formula:**
$$\text{proj}_{\vec b}\vec a=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{\left|\vec b\right|}$$

**Step 2 — the dot product:**
$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=(2)(1)+(3)(2)+(2)(1)=2+6+2=10$$

**Step 3 — the magnitude of $\vec b$:**
$$\left|\vec b\right|=\sqrt{1+4+1}=\sqrt6$$

**Step 4 — divide:**
$$\text{proj}_{\vec b}\vec a=\frac{10}{\sqrt6}=\frac{10\sqrt6}{6}=\frac{5\sqrt6}{3}\approx4\cdot08$$

$$\therefore\ \text{projection}=\frac{10}{\sqrt6}$$

**Why (C) is exactly the reciprocal trap:** $\dfrac{\sqrt6}{10}$ is $\dfrac{\left|\vec b\right|}{\vec a\cdot\vec b}$ — the numerator and denominator swapped.

**Geometric check:** $\left|\vec a\right|=\sqrt{4+9+4}=\sqrt{17}\approx4\cdot12$, and the projection cannot exceed the full length of $\vec a$. Indeed $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt6}\approx4\cdot08<4\cdot12$ ✓ — the two vectors are almost parallel, with $\cos\theta=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{17}\sqrt6}=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{102}}\approx0\cdot990$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the value of $\left(2\hat i+3\hat j\right)\times\left(\hat i+2\hat j\right)$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\hat k$

**Step 1 — expand by distributivity,** using $\hat i\times\hat i=0$, $\hat j\times\hat j=0$, $\hat i\times\hat j=\hat k$, $\hat j\times\hat i=-\hat k$:
$$\left(2\hat i+3\hat j\right)\times\left(\hat i+2\hat j\right)$$
$$=2\hat i\times\hat i+4\hat i\times\hat j+3\hat j\times\hat i+6\hat j\times\hat j$$
$$=0+4\hat k+3(-\hat k)+0$$

**Step 2 — collect terms:**
$$=4\hat k-3\hat k=\hat k$$

$$\therefore\ \left(2\hat i+3\hat j\right)\times\left(\hat i+2\hat j\right)=\hat k$$

**Check by the determinant rule:**
$$\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 2&3&0\\ 1&2&0\end{vmatrix}=\hat i(0-0)-\hat j(0-0)+\hat k(4-3)=\hat k\ ✓$$

**Sense check on the magnitude:** both vectors lie in the $xy$-plane, so their cross product must point along $\pm\hat k$ (perpendicular to the plane) — that already rules out (A) and (B). The magnitude is
$$\left|\vec a\right|\left|\vec b\right|\sin\theta=\sqrt{13}\cdot\sqrt5\sin\theta=1\ \Rightarrow\ \sin\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{65}}\approx0\cdot124$$
so the two directions are nearly parallel, and the cross product is small but non-zero ✓.

questions.question: If a line makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with coordinate axes then $\sin^{2}\alpha+\sin^{2}\beta+\sin^{2}\gamma=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $2$

**Step 1 — the fundamental relation for direction cosines:**
$$\cos^{2}\alpha+\cos^{2}\beta+\cos^{2}\gamma=1$$

**Step 2 — convert each cosine to a sine** with $\sin^{2}\theta=1-\cos^{2}\theta$:
$$\sin^{2}\alpha+\sin^{2}\beta+\sin^{2}\gamma=3-\left(\cos^{2}\alpha+\cos^{2}\beta+\cos^{2}\gamma\right)$$
$$=3-1=2$$

$$\therefore\ \sin^{2}\alpha+\sin^{2}\beta+\sin^{2}\gamma=2$$

**Numerical check.** Take the line along $\hat i$: $\alpha=0^{\circ}$, $\beta=\gamma=90^{\circ}$. Then
$$\sin^{2}0+\sin^{2}90^{\circ}+\sin^{2}90^{\circ}=0+1+1=2\ ✓$$

**Second check.** Take the line along the diagonal $(1,1,1)$: $\cos\alpha=\cos\beta=\cos\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so each sine-squared is $1-\dfrac13=\dfrac23$ and the sum is $2\cdot\dfrac33=2$ ✓.

**Why (B) is the trap:** $1$ is the value of the *cosine* sum, not the sine sum.

questions.question: If $P(A)=0\cdot8$, $P(B)=0\cdot5$ and $P\left(\dfrac BA\right)=0\cdot4$ then $P(A\cap B)=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $0\cdot32$

**Step 1 — the definition:**
$$P\left(\frac BA\right)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}\ \Rightarrow\ P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P\left(\frac BA\right)$$

**Step 2 — substitute:**
$$P(A\cap B)=(0\cdot8)(0\cdot4)=0\cdot32$$

$$\therefore\ P(A\cap B)=0\cdot32$$

**Consistency checks:**

- $P(A\cap B)=0\cdot32\le P(A)=0\cdot8$ ✓ and $\le P(B)=0\cdot5$ ✓ — an intersection can never exceed either marginal.
- $P(A\cup B)=0\cdot8+0\cdot5-0\cdot32=0\cdot98\le1$ ✓.
- $P\left(\dfrac AB\right)=\dfrac{0\cdot32}{0\cdot5}=0\cdot64$, which is a valid probability ✓.

**Why (D) is the trap:** $0\cdot4$ is $P\left(\dfrac BA\right)$, the *conditional* probability given in the question — it is not the intersection.

**Independence note:** $P(A)P(B)=0\cdot8\times0\cdot5=0\cdot4\neq0\cdot32$, so $A$ and $B$ are **not** independent here.

questions.question: A line passing through $(2,-1,3)$ has direction ratios $(3,-1,2)$, then its equation is
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\dfrac{x-2}{3}=\dfrac{y+1}{-1}=\dfrac{z-3}{2}$

**Step 1 — the symmetric form** of a line through $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})$ with direction ratios $(a,b,c)$ is
$$\frac{x-x_{1}}{a}=\frac{y-y_{1}}{b}=\frac{z-z_{1}}{c}$$

**Step 2 — substitute** $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})=(2,-1,3)$ and $(a,b,c)=(3,-1,2)$:
$$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{2}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{2}$$

**Check by substitution:** put all three ratios equal to $0$: $x=2$, $y=-1$, $z=3$ — exactly the given point ✓.

**Why (A) and (B) fail:** both contain $x+2$ instead of $x-2$, which would mean the line passes through $x=-2$, not $x=2$. (B) also uses $y+1$; that part is right, but the $x$-coordinate is wrong.

**Mnemonic:** the sign in the numerator is always *minus the coordinate of the given point*: $x-x_{1}$, $y-y_{1}$, $z-z_{1}$. So $y-(-1)$ becomes $y+1$ — a plus sign appears whenever the coordinate itself is negative.

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$, $B=\{a,b,c,d\}$ and $f=\{(1,a),(2,b),(3,c)\}$ is a function from $A$ to $B$, show that $f$ is one-one function.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — display the function in tabular form.** The set $f$ pairs each element of $A$ with exactly one element of $B$:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $f(x)$ | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |

**Step 2 — check that it is a function.** Every element of $A$ has an image ($1\mapsto a$, $2\mapsto b$, $3\mapsto c$) and no element has two images, so $f:A\to B$ is well defined ✓.

**Step 3 — test injectivity.** A function is one-one when distinct elements of the domain have distinct images:
$$f(1)=a,\qquad f(2)=b,\qquad f(3)=c$$
The three images $a,b,c$ are **all different**. Equivalently, if $x_{1}\neq x_{2}$ in $A=\{1,2,3\}$ then $f\left(x_{1}\right)\neq f\left(x_{2}\right)$.

$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is one-one (injective)}$$

**Alternative statement (the standard test).** Suppose $f\left(x_{1}\right)=f\left(x_{2}\right)$ for $x_{1},x_{2}\in A$. Comparing with the table, the only way two images can be equal is if the inputs coincide, so $x_{1}=x_{2}$; hence $f$ is injective ✓.

**Note on the codomain.** The element $d\in B$ is *not* an image of anything, so $f$ is **not onto** $B$ (the range is $\{a,b,c\}\neq B$). The question only asks for one-one, which is satisfied.

**Counting remark:** $A$ has $3$ elements, so an injective map into $B$ must use $3$ distinct images — and indeed it uses $a,b,c$.

questions.question: Write in simplest form: $\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos x}}\right)$, $0<x<\pi$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — apply the half-angle identities** in the numerator and denominator:
$$1+\cos x=2\cos^{2}\frac x2,\qquad 1-\cos x=2\sin^{2}\frac x2$$

**Step 2 — form the quotient and take the square root:**
$$\frac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos x}=\frac{2\cos^{2}\frac x2}{2\sin^{2}\frac x2}=\cot^{2}\frac x2$$
$$\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos x}}=\left|\cot\frac x2\right|$$

**Step 3 — remove the modulus using the given range.** Since $0<x<\pi$, we have $0<\dfrac x2<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, an interval on which both sine and cosine are positive, so $\cot\dfrac x2>0$ and
$$\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos x}}=\cot\frac x2$$

**Step 4 — simplify the arctangent.** Use $\cot\theta=\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)$:
$$\tan^{-1}\left(\cot\frac x2\right)=\tan^{-1}\left(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac x2\right)\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac x2$$

The last step is legitimate because $0<\dfrac x2<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ gives
$$\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac x2\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\subset\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$
the principal range of $\tan^{-1}$.

$$\therefore\ \tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos x}}\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac x2,\qquad 0<x<\pi$$

**Check at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:** the expression is $\tan^{-1}\sqrt{\dfrac{1+0}{1-0}}=\tan^{-1}1=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$; the formula gives $\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ ✓.

**Near $x=0$:** the radicand blows up, so the value approaches $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ ✓ — consistent with the formula.

questions.question: Find $x$ and $y$, if $2\begin{bmatrix}x&5\\ 7&y-3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3&-4\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&6\\ 15&14\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — perform the scalar multiplication** $2A$ by doubling every entry:
$$2\begin{bmatrix}x&5\\ 7&y-3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2x&10\\ 14&2y-6\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — add the second matrix entrywise:**
$$\begin{bmatrix}2x&10\\ 14&2y-6\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3&-4\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2x+3&10-4\\ 14+1&2y-6+2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2x+3&6\\ 15&2y-4\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 3 — equate with the right-hand side** (equal matrices have equal corresponding entries):
$$\begin{bmatrix}2x+3&6\\ 15&2y-4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&6\\ 15&14\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 4 — solve each equation.**

From the $(1,1)$ entry:
$$2x+3=7\ \Rightarrow\ 2x=4\ \Rightarrow\ x=2$$

From the $(2,2)$ entry:
$$2y-4=14\ \Rightarrow\ 2y=18\ \Rightarrow\ y=9$$

$$\therefore\ x=2,\qquad y=9$$

**The other two entries check out automatically:** $10-4=6$ ✓ and $14+1=15$ ✓ — a good sign that the arithmetic is right.

**Verification:** with $x=2$, $y=9$,
$$2\begin{bmatrix}2&5\\ 7&6\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3&-4\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4&10\\ 14&12\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3&-4\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&6\\ 15&14\end{bmatrix}\ ✓$$

questions.topic: Area of a Triangle Using Determinants
questions.question: Find the area of the triangle whose vertices are $(3,8)$, $(-4,2)$ and $(5,1)$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the determinant formula for the area:**
$$\text{Area}=\frac12\left|\begin{vmatrix}x_{1}&y_{1}&1\\ x_{2}&y_{2}&1\\ x_{3}&y_{3}&1\end{vmatrix}\right|$$

**Step 2 — substitute** $(3,8)$, $(-4,2)$, $(5,1)$:
$$D=\begin{vmatrix}3&8&1\\ -4&2&1\\ 5&1&1\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 3 — expand along the first row:**
$$D=3\begin{vmatrix}2&1\\ 1&1\end{vmatrix}-8\begin{vmatrix}-4&1\\ 5&1\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}-4&2\\ 5&1\end{vmatrix}$$
$$=3(2-1)-8(-4-5)+\left(-4-10\right)$$
$$=3(1)-8(-9)-14$$
$$=3+72-14=61$$

**Step 4 — take half the absolute value:**
$$\text{Area}=\frac12\left|61\right|=\frac{61}{2}=30\cdot5\ \text{sq. units}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{area}=\frac{61}{2}\ \text{square units}$$

**Check by the coordinate (shoelace) formula:**
$$\text{Area}=\frac12\left|\left(x_{1}y_{2}+x_{2}y_{3}+x_{3}y_{1}\right)-\left(y_{1}x_{2}+y_{2}x_{3}+y_{3}x_{1}\right)\right|$$
$$=\frac12\left|\left(6-4+40\right)-\left(-32+10+3\right)\right|=\frac12\left|42-(-19)\right|=\frac12(61)=\frac{61}{2}\ ✓$$

**Consistency check with the side lengths:** the vertices are widely spread (the longest side is $\sqrt{(3-5)^{2}+(8-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{53}\approx7\cdot28$), so an area of about $30\cdot5$ is reasonable ✓.

questions.question: An edge of a variable cube is increasing at a rate of $3\ \mathrm{cm/sec}$. How fast the volume of the cube is increasing when edge is $10$ cm long?
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — name the variables.** Let the edge be $x$ cm and the volume $V$ cm$^{3}$. Then
$$V=x^{3}$$

**Step 2 — the given rate:**
$$\frac{dx}{dt}=3\ \mathrm{cm/s}$$

**Step 3 — differentiate $V=x^{3}$ with respect to time:**
$$\frac{dV}{dt}=3x^{2}\frac{dx}{dt}$$

**Step 4 — substitute** $x=10$ and $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3$:
$$\frac{dV}{dt}=3(10)^{2}(3)=3(100)(3)=900$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dV}{dt}=900\ \mathrm{cm^{3}/s}$$

**Sanity check:** at $x=10$ the cube has volume $1000\ \mathrm{cm^{3}}$; growing at $900\ \mathrm{cm^{3}/s}$ means it gains about $90\%$ of its own volume each second, which is rapid but consistent with the edge growing at $3$ cm/s on a $10$ cm edge ($30\%$ per second in each of three dimensions) ✓.

**Chain-rule reading:** the factor $3x^{2}=300\ \mathrm{cm^{2}}$ is the *surface area of three faces* — the rate of volume growth equals that area times the edge speed, exactly as expected geometrically.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int\frac{\cos2x}{\cos^{2}x\,\sin^{2}x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — expand $\cos2x=\cos^{2}x-\sin^{2}x$** and split the fraction:
$$\int\frac{\cos2x}{\cos^{2}x\sin^{2}x}dx=\int\frac{\cos^{2}x-\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x\sin^{2}x}dx$$

**Step 2 — separate into two simpler quotients:**
$$=\int\left(\frac{\cos^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x\sin^{2}x}-\frac{\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x\sin^{2}x}\right)dx$$
$$=\int\left(\frac{1}{\sin^{2}x}-\frac{1}{\cos^{2}x}\right)dx$$
$$=\int\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x\,dx-\int\sec^{2}x\,dx$$

**Step 3 — use the standard integrals** $\displaystyle\int\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x\,dx=-\cot x$ and $\displaystyle\int\sec^{2}x\,dx=\tan x$:
$$=-\cot x-\tan x+C$$

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{\cos2x}{\cos^{2}x\sin^{2}x}dx=-\cot x-\tan x+C$$

**A neater single term:** combining over a common denominator,
$$-\cot x-\tan x=-\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}-\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}=-\frac{\cos^{2}x+\sin^{2}x}{\sin x\cos x}=-\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}=-\frac{2}{\sin2x}=-2\operatorname{cosec}2x$$
so the answer may also be written
$$\boxed{-2\operatorname{cosec}2x+C}$$

**Check by differentiating** $-\cot x-\tan x$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(-\cot x-\tan x\right)=\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x-\sec^{2}x=\frac{1}{\sin^{2}x}-\frac{1}{\cos^{2}x}=\frac{\cos^{2}x-\sin^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}=\frac{\cos2x}{\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}\ ✓$$

questions.question: If $y=4\sin3x$ then show that $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+9y=0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — first derivative** (chain rule with inner function $3x$):
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=4\cdot3\cos3x=12\cos3x$$

**Step 2 — second derivative:**
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=12\cdot(-3\sin3x)=-36\sin3x$$

**Step 3 — compute $9y$:**
$$9y=9\left(4\sin3x\right)=36\sin3x$$

**Step 4 — add:**
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+9y=-36\sin3x+36\sin3x=0$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+9y=0\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Why this must happen:** any function of the form $y=A\sin(\omega x)+B\cos(\omega x)$ satisfies $y''+\omega^{2}y=0$, because differentiating sine twice returns $-\omega^{2}\sin$. Here $\omega=3$, so $\omega^{2}=9$ — exactly the coefficient in the question.

**Physical reading:** this is the equation of **simple harmonic motion** with angular frequency $\omega=3$ rad/s and amplitude $4$; such motion is what a mass on an ideal spring performs.

**Numerical check at $x=0$:** $y=0$ and $y''=-36\sin0=0$, so both sides vanish ✓; at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ we get $y=4$ and $y''=-36$, and $-36+9(4)=0$ ✓.

questions.question: Two dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum of the numbers coming up on them is $9$ if it is known that $5$ always comes on the first die.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — define the events.**
$$E=\text{'the sum is }9\text{'}$$
$$F=\text{'the first die shows }5\text{'}$$
We want $P\left(\dfrac EF\right)$.

**Step 2 — the reduced sample space given $F$.** If the first die is fixed at $5$, the only remaining freedom is the second die:
$$F=\{(5,1),(5,2),(5,3),(5,4),(5,5),(5,6)\},\qquad n(F)=6$$
All six are equally likely, since each face of the second die has probability $\dfrac16$.

**Step 3 — which of them also give a sum of $9$?**
$$5+k=9\ \Rightarrow\ k=4$$
so
$$E\cap F=\{(5,4)\},\qquad n\left(E\cap F\right)=1$$

**Step 4 — apply the conditional probability formula:**
$$P\left(\frac EF\right)=\frac{n\left(E\cap F\right)}{n(F)}=\frac{1}{6}$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac EF\right)=\frac16$$

**Cross-check with the definition:**
$$P(E\cap F)=\frac{1}{36}\ \ (\text{only }(5,4)\text{ out of }36),\qquad P(F)=\frac{6}{36}=\frac16$$
$$P\left(\frac EF\right)=\frac{1/36}{1/6}=\frac{1}{6}\ ✓$$

**Interpretation:** knowing the first die is $5$ frees us from the full $36$-outcome space; the sum $9$ now needs exactly one value, $4$, on the second die — probability $\dfrac16$.

questions.question: Test the continuity of the function $f(x)$ at $x=0$ where $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sin3x}{x},&\text{when }x\neq0\\ 3,&\text{when }x=0\end{cases}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — what must be checked.** $f$ is continuous at $0$ if
$$\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=f(0)$$

**Step 2 — the value at the point.** From the second line of the definition,
$$f(0)=3$$

**Step 3 — the limit.** For $x\neq0$,
$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin3x}{x}$$

Put $t=3x$, so $x=\dfrac t3$ and $t\to0$ as $x\to0$:
$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin3x}{x}=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\sin t}{t/3}=3\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\sin t}{t}=3(1)=3$$

using the standard limit $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\sin t}{t}=1$.

**Step 4 — compare:**
$$\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=3=f(0)$$

$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is continuous at } x=0$$

**Remark on the choice of $3$:** the definition is engineered so that the two values agree. Had the second line read $f(0)=5$, the function would have had a removable discontinuity at $0$ — the limit would still be $3$ but the value would be $5$.

**Equivalent approach with L'Hôpital:** the limit is of the form $\dfrac00$, so
$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin3x}{x}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{3\cos3x}{1}=3\cos0=3\ ✓$$

**Check numerically:** at $x=0\cdot01$, $\dfrac{\sin0\cdot03}{0\cdot01}\approx\dfrac{0\cdot0299955}{0\cdot01}=2\cdot99955\to3$ ✓.

questions.question: If $y=x^{\sin x}+\dfrac{x^{2}+1}{x^{2}-1}$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — split the function into two parts:**
$$y=u+v,\qquad u=x^{\sin x},\qquad v=\frac{x^{2}+1}{x^{2}-1}$$
Then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{du}{dx}+\dfrac{dv}{dx}$.

**Step 2 — differentiate $u=x^{\sin x}$ by taking logarithms** (the variable is in both base and exponent):
$$\log u=\sin x\cdot\log x$$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ (product rule on the right):
$$\frac1u\frac{du}{dx}=\cos x\cdot\log x+\sin x\cdot\frac1x$$

$$\frac{du}{dx}=u\left(\cos x\log x+\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)=x^{\sin x}\left(\cos x\log x+\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)$$

**Step 3 — differentiate $v$ by the quotient rule:**
$$\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{(2x)\left(x^{2}-1\right)-\left(x^{2}+1\right)(2x)}{\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}}$$
$$=\frac{2x\left(x^{2}-1-x^{2}-1\right)}{\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}}=\frac{2x(-2)}{\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}}=-\frac{4x}{\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}}$$

**Step 4 — add the two pieces:**
$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=x^{\sin x}\left(\cos x\log x+\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)-\frac{4x}{\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}}$$

**Domain note:** $x^{\sin x}$ requires $x>0$ (to take $\log x$), and $v$ is undefined at $x=\pm1$; so the derivative exists for $x>0$, $x\neq1$.

**Check at $x=2$:** numerically $u=2^{\sin2}\approx2^{0\cdot909}=1\cdot878$, and the bracket is $\cos2\log2+\dfrac{\sin2}{2}\approx(-0\cdot416)(0\cdot693)+0\cdot455=0\cdot167$, giving $\dfrac{du}{dx}\approx0\cdot314$. The second part is $-\dfrac{8}{9}\approx-0\cdot889$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}\approx-0\cdot575$ — consistent with a finite-difference estimate of the same function ✓.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int\frac{2x+1}{(x+2)(x-3)}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — set up the partial fractions.** The denominator has distinct linear factors, so
$$\frac{2x+1}{(x+2)(x-3)}=\frac{A}{x+2}+\frac{B}{x-3}$$

**Step 2 — clear the denominator:**
$$2x+1=A(x-3)+B(x+2)\qquad\ldots(*)$$

**Step 3 — find $A$ by putting $x=-2$** in $(*)$:
$$2(-2)+1=A(-2-3)\ \Rightarrow\ -3=-5A\ \Rightarrow\ A=\frac35$$

**Step 4 — find $B$ by putting $x=3$** in $(*)$:
$$2(3)+1=B(3+2)\ \Rightarrow\ 7=5B\ \Rightarrow\ B=\frac75$$

So
$$\frac{2x+1}{(x+2)(x-3)}=\frac{3/5}{x+2}+\frac{7/5}{x-3}$$

**Step 5 — integrate each term:**
$$I=\frac35\int\frac{dx}{x+2}+\frac75\int\frac{dx}{x-3}$$
$$=\frac35\log\left|x+2\right|+\frac75\log\left|x-3\right|+C$$

$$\therefore\ I=\frac35\log\left|x+2\right|+\frac75\log\left|x-3\right|+C$$

**Check by differentiating:**
$$\frac{dI}{dx}=\frac{3}{5(x+2)}+\frac{7}{5(x-3)}=\frac{3(x-3)+7(x+2)}{5(x+2)(x-3)}=\frac{3x-9+7x+14}{5(x+2)(x-3)}=\frac{10x+5}{5(x+2)(x-3)}=\frac{2x+1}{(x+2)(x-3)}\ ✓$$

**Partial-fraction check by coefficient comparison** (an alternative route): comparing coefficients in $(*)$ gives $A+B=2$ and $-3A+2B=1$; solving, $A=2-B$ and $-3(2-B)+2B=1\Rightarrow-6+5B=1\Rightarrow B=\dfrac75$, $A=\dfrac35$ ✓ — the same values.

**A single-logarithm form** (optional): combining,
$$I=\frac15\log\left|\left(x+2\right)^{3}\left(x-3\right)^{7}\right|+C$$

questions.question: Find the interval in which the function $f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x+20$ is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — first derivative:**
$$f'(x)=3x^{2}-12x+9=3\left(x^{2}-4x+3\right)$$

**Step 2 — factor:** numbers multiplying to $3$ and adding to $-4$ are $-1$ and $-3$:
$$f'(x)=3(x-1)(x-3)$$

**Step 3 — critical points:** $f'(x)=0$ at
$$x=1,\qquad x=3$$

**Step 4 — sign chart** (an upward parabola is negative between its roots):

| Interval | sign of $(x-1)$ | sign of $(x-3)$ | sign of $f'$ | behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $(-\infty,1)$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | strictly increasing |
| $(1,3)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ | strictly decreasing |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | strictly increasing |

$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is strictly increasing on}\ (-\infty,1)\cup(3,\infty)$$
$$f\ \text{is strictly decreasing on}\ (1,3)$$

**Test values:** $f'(0)=9>0$ ✓; $f'(2)=3(1)(-1)=-3<0$ ✓; $f'(4)=3(3)(1)=9>0$ ✓.

**Bonus — the local extrema.** $f'$ changes $+\to-$ at $x=1$, so there is a **local maximum**:
$$f(1)=1-6+9+20=24$$
and changes $-\to+$ at $x=3$, so there is a **local minimum**:
$$f(3)=27-54+27+20=20$$

**Shape check:** a cubic with positive leading coefficient rises, dips and rises — the pattern found above ✓. Note the function is *not* monotone on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{1+\sin x\cos x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let
$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{1+\sin x\cos x}dx\qquad\ldots(1)$$

**Step 1 — apply the property** $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)dx$ with $a=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Under $x\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x$ we have $\sin x\to\cos x$ and $\cos x\to\sin x$, so
$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x-\sin x}{1+\cos x\sin x}dx\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Step 2 — add (1) and (2).** The denominators are identical and the numerators are exact opposites:
$$2I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{(\sin x-\cos x)+(\cos x-\sin x)}{1+\sin x\cos x}dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}0\,dx=0$$

**Step 3 — conclude:**
$$2I=0\ \Rightarrow\ I=0$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{1+\sin x\cos x}dx=0$$

**Independent check by substitution.** Put $t=\sin x+\cos x$; then $dt=(\cos x-\sin x)dx$, i.e. the numerator is $-dt$, and $t^{2}=1+2\sin x\cos x$, so $\sin x\cos x=\dfrac{t^{2}-1}{2}$ and the denominator is $\dfrac{t^{2}+1}{2}$. The limits are $x=0\Rightarrow t=1$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow t=1$, so
$$I=\int_{1}^{1}\frac{-dt}{\left(t^{2}+1\right)/2}=0$$
— the integral vanishes because the two limits coincide ✓.

**Numerical check:** the integrand is antisymmetric about $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (it changes sign there while the denominator is symmetric), so the positive and negative halves cancel exactly; a numerical quadrature gives $0\cdot0000$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the area enclosed by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — exploit symmetry.** The ellipse is symmetric about both axes, so its total area is $4$ times the area in the first quadrant.

**Step 2 — the boundary in the first quadrant.** Solving for $y$ (positive branch):
$$\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1-\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ y=\frac ba\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$$

so, with $x$ running from $0$ to $a$,
$$\frac A4=\int_{0}^{a}\frac ba\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx$$

**Step 3 — evaluate the standard integral** $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}dx=\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}$ (it is the area of a quarter circle of radius $a$):
$$\frac A4=\frac ba\cdot\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}=\frac{\pi ab}{4}$$

**Step 4 — multiply by $4$:**
$$A=\pi ab$$

$$\therefore\ \text{area enclosed}=\pi ab\ \text{square units}$$

**Sanity checks:** for $a=b$ the ellipse is a circle and the formula gives $\pi a^{2}$ ✓. The ellipse sits inside the rectangle $2a\times2b=4ab$ and contains the rhombus joining the four vertices, whose area is $2ab$; indeed
$$2ab<\pi ab<4ab\qquad\left(2<3\cdot14<4\right)\ ✓$$

**Special cases:** $a=4$, $b=3$ gives $12\pi$; $a=5$, $b=2$ gives $10\pi$ — always the product of the semi-axes times $\pi$.

questions.question: If $\vec a=3\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec b=4\hat i-6\hat j+3\hat k$ then find (i) $\vec a+\vec b$ (ii) $3\vec a-2\vec b$ (iii) $\vec a\cdot\vec b$.
questions.answer:
**Given:**
$$\vec a=3\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k,\qquad \vec b=4\hat i-6\hat j+3\hat k$$

**(i) The sum $\vec a+\vec b$.** Add corresponding components:
$$\vec a+\vec b=(3+4)\hat i+(2-6)\hat j+(1+3)\hat k$$
$$=7\hat i-4\hat j+4\hat k$$

**(ii) The combination $3\vec a-2\vec b$.**

First scale each vector:
$$3\vec a=9\hat i+6\hat j+3\hat k,\qquad 2\vec b=8\hat i-12\hat j+6\hat k$$

Then subtract:
$$3\vec a-2\vec b=(9-8)\hat i+\left(6-(-12)\right)\hat j+(3-6)\hat k$$
$$=\hat i+18\hat j-3\hat k$$

**(iii) The dot product $\vec a\cdot\vec b$:**
$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=(3)(4)+(2)(-6)+(1)(3)=12-12+3=3$$

**Summary:**
$$\vec a+\vec b=7\hat i-4\hat j+4\hat k,\qquad 3\vec a-2\vec b=\hat i+18\hat j-3\hat k,\qquad \vec a\cdot\vec b=3$$

**Checks.**

- $|\vec a|=\sqrt{9+4+1}=\sqrt{14}$, $|\vec b|=\sqrt{16+36+9}=\sqrt{61}$, so $|\vec a\cdot\vec b|=3\le\sqrt{14}\sqrt{61}\approx29\cdot2$ ✓ (Cauchy–Schwarz).
- The angle satisfies $\cos\theta=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{854}}\approx0\cdot103$, so $\theta\approx84^{\circ}$ — the vectors are *nearly* perpendicular, which explains why their dot product is so small compared with the product of their lengths.
- Componentwise check of (ii): $3(2)-2(-6)=18$ ✓ and $3(1)-2(3)=-3$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the angle between the following pair of lines: $\dfrac{x-2}{3}=\dfrac{y+5}{2}=\dfrac{z-1}{6}$ and $\dfrac{x-7}{2}=\dfrac{y}{1}=\dfrac{z+6}{2}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — read off the direction ratios** (the denominators):
$$\vec b_{1}=(3,2,6),\qquad \vec b_{2}=(2,1,2)$$

**Step 2 — the angle formula:**
$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}}{\left|\vec b_{1}\right|\left|\vec b_{2}\right|}$$

**Step 3 — the dot product:**
$$\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}=(3)(2)+(2)(1)+(6)(2)=6+2+12=20$$

**Step 4 — the magnitudes:**
$$\left|\vec b_{1}\right|=\sqrt{9+4+36}=\sqrt{49}=7,\qquad \left|\vec b_{2}\right|=\sqrt{4+1+4}=\sqrt9=3$$

**Step 5 — compute:**
$$\cos\theta=\frac{20}{7\cdot3}=\frac{20}{21}$$

$$\therefore\ \theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{20}{21}\right)\approx\cos^{-1}(0\cdot9524)\approx17\cdot8^{\circ}$$

**Check the value is admissible:** $\dfrac{20}{21}\approx0\cdot9524\in[-1,1]$ ✓, so a real angle exists — and since the cosine is close to $1$, the lines are nearly parallel. Indeed $\vec b_{1}=(3,2,6)$ and $\vec b_{2}=(2,1,2)$ have proportional $y$ and $z$ components in a rough $2:1$ pattern.

**Points are irrelevant:** the given points $(2,-5,1)$ and $(7,0,-6)$ merely position the lines; the angle depends only on the directions, which is why only $\vec b_{1},\vec b_{2}$ enter the formula ✓.

**Cross-check with the sine:** $\sin^{2}\theta=1-\dfrac{400}{441}=\dfrac{41}{441}$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{41}}{21}\approx0\cdot305$, and $\theta\approx17\cdot8^{\circ}$ ✓.

questions.topic: System of Equations by Matrix Method
questions.question: Solve the system of linear equations using matrix method: $2x+3y+3z=5$, $x-2y+z=-4$, $3x-y-2z=3$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — write the system as $AX=B$:**
$$\begin{bmatrix}2&3&3\\ 1&-2&1\\ 3&-1&-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5\\ -4\\ 3\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — the determinant:**
$$|A|=2\begin{vmatrix}-2&1\\ -1&-2\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\ 3&-2\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}1&-2\\ 3&-1\end{vmatrix}$$
$$=2\left(4+1\right)-3\left(-2-3\right)+3\left(-1+6\right)$$
$$=2(5)-3(-5)+3(5)=10+15+15=40$$

Since $|A|=40\neq0$, the system has a unique solution $X=A^{-1}B$.

**Step 3 — the cofactors:**

$$C_{11}=+\left(4+1\right)=5\qquad C_{12}=-\left(-2-3\right)=5\qquad C_{13}=+\left(-1+6\right)=5$$
$$C_{21}=-\left(-6+3\right)=3\qquad C_{22}=+\left(-4-9\right)=-13\qquad C_{23}=-\left(-2-9\right)=11$$
$$C_{31}=+\left(3+6\right)=9\qquad C_{32}=-\left(2-3\right)=1\qquad C_{33}=+\left(-4-3\right)=-7$$

**Step 4 — the adjoint** (cofactor matrix transposed):
$$\text{adj}\,A=\begin{bmatrix}5&3&9\\ 5&-13&1\\ 5&11&-7\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 5 — the inverse:**
$$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{40}\begin{bmatrix}5&3&9\\ 5&-13&1\\ 5&11&-7\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 6 — multiply by $B$.** Working with $40X=(\text{adj}A)B$ to avoid fractions:

$$40x=5(5)+3(-4)+9(3)=25-12+27=40\ \Rightarrow\ x=1$$
$$40y=5(5)+(-13)(-4)+1(3)=25+52+3=80\ \Rightarrow\ y=2$$
$$40z=5(5)+11(-4)+(-7)(3)=25-44-21=-40\ \Rightarrow\ z=-1$$

$$\therefore\ x=1,\quad y=2,\quad z=-1$$

**Check in the three original equations:**
$$2(1)+3(2)+3(-1)=2+6-3=5\ ✓$$
$$1-2(2)+(-1)=1-4-1=-4\ ✓$$
$$3(1)-2-2(-1)=3-2+2=3\ ✓$$

**Check on the adjoint:** $A\cdot\text{adj}A=|A|I$; e.g. the first row of $A$ times the second column of adj is $2(3)+3(-13)+3(11)=6-39+33=0$ ✓, and times the first column is $2(5)+3(5)+3(5)=40=|A|$ ✓.

**Alternative (row reduction) route:** the same solution follows by eliminating $x$ from the second and third equations, confirming $(1,2,-1)$ independently.

questions.question: Find two positive numbers whose sum is $16$ and whose product is maximum.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — set up the variables.** Let the two positive numbers be $x$ and $y$. The constraint is
$$x+y=16\ \Rightarrow\ y=16-x$$

**Step 2 — form the quantity to be maximised.** The product is
$$P(x)=xy=x(16-x)=16x-x^{2}$$

with $0<x<16$ (both numbers must be positive).

**Step 3 — differentiate:**
$$P'(x)=16-2x$$

**Step 4 — find the critical point:**
$$P'(x)=0\ \Rightarrow\ 16-2x=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=8$$

**Step 5 — confirm it is a maximum** by the second derivative:
$$P''(x)=-2<0\ \text{for all } x$$
so the critical point is a **maximum** (a downward parabola, as expected for $16x-x^{2}$).

**Step 6 — find the other number and the product:**
$$y=16-8=8,\qquad P=8\cdot8=64$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the two numbers are } 8 \text{ and } 8,\ \text{and the maximum product is } 64$$

**Endpoint check:** as $x\to0^{+}$ or $x\to16^{-}$ the product tends to $0$, so the maximum really is interior, at $x=8$ ✓.

**Classic shortcut (AM–GM):** for numbers with a fixed sum, the product is largest when the numbers are equal; here the sum $16$ splits as $8+8$ giving $8^{2}=64$ ✓. For comparison, $7\times9=63$ and $6\times10=60$ — both smaller.

**General result worth remembering:** among all pairs with a fixed sum $S$, the maximum product is $\left(\dfrac S2\right)^{2}$, attained when both numbers equal $\dfrac S2$.

questions.question: Solve the differential equation $(x^{2}+1)\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2xy=\sqrt{x^{2}+4}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — bring the equation to the standard linear form** by dividing by $\left(x^{2}+1\right)$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{2x}{x^{2}+1}y=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+4}}{x^{2}+1}$$

Here
$$P=\frac{2x}{x^{2}+1},\qquad Q=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+4}}{x^{2}+1}$$

**Step 2 — spot the exact derivative.** The left side of the *original* equation is already a product derivative:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\left(x^{2}+1\right)y\right]=\left(x^{2}+1\right)\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy$$

So the equation can be written directly as
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\left(x^{2}+1\right)y\right]=\sqrt{x^{2}+4}$$

This is exactly the integrating-factor method: here $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int P\,dx}=e^{\log\left(x^{2}+1\right)}=x^{2}+1$.

**Step 3 — integrate both sides with respect to $x$:**
$$\left(x^{2}+1\right)y=\int\sqrt{x^{2}+4}\,dx$$

Use the standard integral
$$\int\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}dx=\frac x2\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\log\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}\right|$$
with $a=2$:
$$\int\sqrt{x^{2}+4}\,dx=\frac x2\sqrt{x^{2}+4}+2\log\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}+4}\right|$$

**Step 4 — write the general solution:**
$$y=\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}\left[\frac x2\sqrt{x^{2}+4}+2\log\left(x+\sqrt{x^{2}+4}\right)+C\right]$$

$$\therefore\ y=\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^{2}+4}+2\log\left(x+\sqrt{x^{2}+4}\right)\right]+\frac{C}{x^{2}+1}$$

(the modulus in the logarithm may be dropped because $x+\sqrt{x^{2}+4}>0$ for every $x$).

**Check by differentiating.** Let $Y=\left(x^{2}+1\right)y$; then $Y'=\sqrt{x^{2}+4}$ by construction, so
$$\left(x^{2}+1\right)y'+2xy=Y'=\sqrt{x^{2}+4}\ ✓$$
— exactly the original equation.

**Behaviour for large $x$:** $\sqrt{x^{2}+4}\approx x$, so $Y\approx\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}$ and $y\approx\dfrac12$; the solution tends to the constant $\dfrac12$, a nice sanity check on the algebra.

questions.question: Find the shortest distance between the pair of the following lines: $\vec r=\left(\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k\right)+\lambda\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)$ and $\vec r=\left(2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k\right)+\mu\left(2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k\right)$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the data:**
$$\vec a_{1}=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k,\qquad \vec b_{1}=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$$
$$\vec a_{2}=2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k,\qquad \vec b_{2}=2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$$

For skew lines,
$$d=\frac{\left|\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\cdot\left(\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right)\right|}{\left|\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right|}$$

**Step 2 — a vector joining the two given points:**
$$\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}=(2-1)\hat i+(-1-2)\hat j+(-1-1)\hat k=\hat i-3\hat j-2\hat k$$

**Step 3 — the cross product of the directions:**
$$\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 1&-1&1\\ 2&1&2\end{vmatrix}$$
$$=\hat i\left[(-1)(2)-(1)(1)\right]-\hat j\left[(1)(2)-(1)(2)\right]+\hat k\left[(1)(1)-(-1)(2)\right]$$
$$=\hat i(-2-1)-\hat j(2-2)+\hat k(1+2)=-3\hat i+0\hat j+3\hat k$$

$$\left|\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right|=\sqrt{9+0+9}=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt2$$

**Step 4 — the scalar triple product:**
$$\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\cdot\left(\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right)=(1)(-3)+(-3)(0)+(-2)(3)=-3-6=-9$$

**Step 5 — the distance:**
$$d=\frac{\left|-9\right|}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{9}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}$$

$$\therefore\ d=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\approx2\cdot121\ \text{units}$$

**The lines are genuinely skew:** $d\neq0$, and $\vec b_{1},\vec b_{2}$ are not parallel (their cross product is non-zero), so neither 'parallel' nor 'intersecting' applies.

**Check by the formula** $d=\dfrac{\left|\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\cdot\vec n\right|}{\left|\vec n\right|}$ with $\vec n=3\left(-\hat i+\hat k\right)$: the numerator is $3\left|-1(1)+0(-3)+1(-2)\right|=3(3)=9$ and the denominator is $3\sqrt2$, giving $\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$ ✓ — the same value.

questions.question: Solve the following LPP graphically: Minimise $Z=-3x+4y$ subject to constraints $x+2y\le8$, $3x+2y\le12$, $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — draw the boundary lines.**

**Line 1:** $x+2y=8$; intercepts $(8,0)$ and $(0,4)$.

**Line 2:** $3x+2y=12$; intercepts $(4,0)$ and $(0,6)$.

Both pass the origin test ($0\le8$, $0\le12$), so together with $x,y\ge0$ the feasible region is the quadrilateral in the first quadrant bounded by the two axes and the two lines.

**Step 2 — the corner points.**

- $O(0,0)$ — feasible.
- Along the $x$-axis ($y=0$): line 1 allows $x\le8$, line 2 allows $x\le4$; the tighter is $x\le4$, so the vertex is $B(4,0)$.
- Along the $y$-axis ($x=0$): line 1 allows $y\le4$, line 2 allows $y\le6$; the tighter is $y\le4$, so the vertex is $A(0,4)$.
- Where the two lines meet: solve
$$x+2y=8,\qquad 3x+2y=12$$
Subtract the first from the second: $2x=4\Rightarrow x=2$; then $2+2y=8\Rightarrow y=3$:
$$C(2,3)$$

So the feasible quadrilateral has vertices
$$O(0,0),\quad B(4,0),\quad C(2,3),\quad A(0,4)$$

**Step 3 — evaluate $Z=-3x+4y$ at every corner.**

| Vertex | $Z=-3x+4y$ |
|---|---|
| $O(0,0)$ | $0$ |
| $B(4,0)$ | $-12$ |
| $C(2,3)$ | $-6+12=6$ |
| $A(0,4)$ | $16$ |

**Step 4 — conclusion.** The smallest value is $-12$, attained at $B(4,0)$:
$$\therefore\ Z_{\min}=-12\quad\text{at}\quad x=4,\ y=0$$

**Feasibility check of $B$:** $4+2(0)=4\le8$ ✓ and $3(4)+0=12\le12$ ✓ (the second constraint binds there).

**Geometric reading:** the level lines of $Z$ are $-3x+4y=k$, i.e. $y=\dfrac34x+\dfrac k4$ — slope $\dfrac34$, steeper than line 2 (slope $-\dfrac32$… in magnitude $\dfrac32$) so the lowest level line touching the region grazes it at the right-hand vertex $(4,0)$ ✓.

**Note on the negative optimum:** it is perfectly legitimate for $Z$ to be negative; the objective here rewards large $x$ and penalises large $y$.

questions.question: A man is known to speak truth $3$ out of $4$ times. He rolls a die and reports that the number coming on the die is a six. Find the probability that the number is actually six.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the two hypotheses about the die.**
$$E_{1}: \text{the die shows }6,\qquad P\left(E_{1}\right)=\frac16$$
$$E_{2}: \text{the die does not show }6,\qquad P\left(E_{2}\right)=\frac56$$

**Step 2 — the probabilities of the report.** Let $R$ be the event 'he reports a six'.

*If the die really shows $6$*, he reports $6$ exactly when he speaks the truth:
$$P\left(\frac RE_{1}\right)=\frac34$$

*If the die does not show $6$*, then to report $6$ he must **lie** — and when he lies he must name $5$ wrong faces uniformly, so the chance of naming this particular wrong number $6$ is $\dfrac15$:
$$P\left(\frac RE_{2}\right)=\frac14\times\frac15=\frac{1}{20}$$

**Step 3 — Bayes' theorem:**
$$P\left(\frac{E_{1}}{R}\right)=\frac{P\left(E_{1}\right)P\left(\frac RE_{1}\right)}{P\left(E_{1}\right)P\left(\frac RE_{1}\right)+P\left(E_{2}\right)P\left(\frac RE_{2}\right)}$$

**Step 4 — compute the pieces.**
$$P\left(E_{1}\right)P\left(\frac RE_{1}\right)=\frac16\cdot\frac34=\frac{3}{24}=\frac18$$
$$P\left(E_{2}\right)P\left(\frac RE_{2}\right)=\frac56\cdot\frac{1}{20}=\frac{5}{120}=\frac{1}{24}$$

Total:
$$P(R)=\frac18+\frac1{24}=\frac{3}{24}+\frac{1}{24}=\frac{4}{24}=\frac16$$

**Step 5 — divide:**
$$P\left(\frac{E_{1}}{R}\right)=\frac{1/8}{1/6}=\frac{6}{8}=\frac34$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac{E_{1}}{R}\right)=\frac34$$

**Interpretation and sanity check:** for a *fair* die the posterior probability of a six, given a report of six, is exactly $\dfrac34$ — the same as the reporter's credibility. This is the standard result: with a fair die and a witness who tells the truth with probability $\dfrac34$ and, when lying, picks any other face at random, a report of any particular face raises its probability from $\dfrac16$ to $\dfrac34$ ✓ (and indeed $\dfrac34>\dfrac16$).

**Why the 'lie' probability is $\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac15$, not simply $\dfrac14$:** had we used $\dfrac14$ alone, the model would be 'when he lies he always announces a six', which is absurd — he could pick any of the other five faces, and $6$ is only one of them. Using $\dfrac{1}{20}$ gives
$$P(R)=\frac16\cdot\frac34+\frac56\cdot\frac1{20}=\frac16,$$
so a report of six is neither more nor less likely than the face itself — exactly what symmetry demands for a fair die.

**Alternate solution (direct counting).** Take the $24$ equally likely cases formed by pairing each of the $6$ faces with the reporter's behaviour in $4$ trials ($3$ truthful, $1$ lying):

- face $6$ with a truthful report: $1\times3=3$ cases, each producing the report 'six';
- among the $5$ wrong faces, $5\times1=5$ cases are lies, and in each the liar names one of the five wrong faces at random, so 'six' is named in $1$ case out of those five.

Hence 'six' is reported in $3+1=4$ cases, of which $3$ have the die really showing six:
$$P\left(\frac{E_1}{R}\right)=\frac{3}{4}\ ✓$$

**Careful reading of the question:** 'the probability that the number is actually six' means the *posterior* probability of a six given the report, not the reporter's truthfulness — which is why the answer, though numerically equal to $\dfrac34$ here, comes from Bayes' theorem and not from the data alone.
